title: BLACKWOOD
description: By day, you run a DVD store in 2012 New York. By night, you’re a ruthless assassin. BLACKWOOD is a cinematic third-person shooter with grounded melee combat, brutal takedowns, responsive gunplay, and a double life to manage.

letsplay.title: BLACKWOOD Is The Game I've Been Waiting For

conclusion.summary: Блогер считает BLACKWOOD крайне интересной игрой благодаря её уникальной концепции: контрасту между повседневной жизнью владельца магазина DVD и деятельностью наемного убийцы. Он отмечает, что игра не пытается переизобрести жанр шутера, а фокусируется на синергии двух разных игровых циклов — симулятора жизни и кинематографичного экшена. Блогеру особенно импонирует идея «двойной жизни» героя, где рутинные действия имеют сюжетное значение и влияют на прогрессию.

conclusion.verdict: BLACKWOOD выделяется на фоне других игр за счет смелого сочетания симулятора магазина и экшена. Блогер высоко оценивает проработку механик, где управление бизнесом напрямую влияет на прогрессию и идентичность персонажа. Игра успешно передает атмосферу двойной жизни, делая каждый момент — от продажи DVD до кровавых контрактов — значимым для истории.

segments.text: There's something that we've seen a thousand times in games. You're a killer, you're a soldier, you're a criminal. You finish the mission, you collect your money and you upgrade your weapons. And then the game asks you to do it all over again. But Blackwood has a strange idea. What if, after killing someone, you have to go home and run a DVD store? What if your character wasn't just an assassin?

What if he actually had a life? By day, Anton Blackwood is an ordinary shopkeeper in 2012 New York. He sells DVDs, he manages stock and he talks to customers. Then he goes home, he gets dressed and he lives what looks like a completely normal life. And then night comes and he goes downstairs, opens up the black market, gets his weapons and takes a contract.

and then becomes something completely different. BLACKWOOD isn't really about being an assassin. It's about trying to convince yourself that you aren't one. And the more I look at this game, the more I think that the strange contradiction could be what makes it so interesting. But first up, let's get the obvious comparison out the way. BLACKWOOD looks like John Wick, yes.

The third-person perspective, the gunplay, the diving, the rolling, the close-quarters combat and the brutal takedowns. Even some of the marketing has leaned into that comparison. And I completely understand why. But if that's all that BLACKWOOD was, I don't think we'd be talking about it. Because we've played games where you're an unstoppable killing machine before. What we haven't played nearly as often is a game that asks what happens before and after the killing.

And being a fan of these sort of games, that's the part that interests me. Because Blackwood doesn't just want you to experience his violence, he wants you to experience the life he's trying to hide from it. And that's a much more interesting premise. Anton isn't introduced as some larger-than-life action hero. He's a DVD store owner. And that's almost funny when you put it next to what he does at night. During the day, you're worrying about inventory, customers and your prices.

You're worried about your store, your apartment, your relationships. And then the sun goes down. And suddenly, you're worried about ammo, weapons, and contracts. And whether you're actually going to make it home alive. The developers describe Blackwood as a story about a man living between these two worlds. And the game's entire structure revolves around that contrast. You wake up, you get ready, and you open the shop. You run your business. And then you leave for a mission.

You come back, you upgrade your equipment, you make your decisions, and eventually you sleep. It's almost like two completely different games have been stitched together. A small life simulator, and a cinematic action thriller. But the important part is, they're not supposed to be separate. They're supposed to feed into each other. Learn very early where to stand. This is where Blackwood really starts to become more than a gimmick, because the DVD store isn't just somewhere you go between missions,

It's part of your progression. You can restock it, organise inventory, set the prices and even work the counter yourself. Or you can let your assistant handle customers while you focus elsewhere. Slow day. Even the dust is bored. Want me to entertain it? Please don't. And there's an actual economic difference depending on how much effort you put in. If you barely manage the store, you're looking at roughly $60 to $80 a day.

But if you actively run it properly, that can rise to $500 or more. And suddenly your day job actually matters because Anton has bills. He has expenses. And he has something far more interesting than a standard currency system. He has two kinds of money. Clean money and dirty money. Clean cash comes from the legitimate side of Anton's life. The store, normal work and even certain missions. It's what keeps his civilian existence running along.

Dirty cash, however, comes from the other side. From your contracts, your weapons and your black market upgrades. And the game even has a system where part of your daily legitimate income is effectively pulled from your dirty earnings. You're laundering your own money just to keep pretending you're normal. Think about what Blackwood is actually asking you to balance. If you spend too much time working, you might be neglecting the other side of his life. And if you focus on contracts, you're making more dirty money

But you're also spending more time becoming the person who earns it. If you invest in the store, you're strengthening Anton's legitimate identity. If you invest in weapons and combat upgrades, you're strengthening the assassin. And neither side completely replaces the other. And that's important, because this isn't a simple morality system where the game eventually asks, are you good or are you evil? It's much more uncomfortable than that. Anton needs both lives.

The clean money keeps his normal life going and the dirty money funds the violence that makes everything else possible. The more you play, the harder it becomes to separate the two. But, of course, none of this matters if the actual action isn't satisfying. And this is where Blackwood is clearly trying to go all in. The combat is built around movement. You've got dive, rolls, slides, cover, gunplay and close quarters encounters.

But the thing that really caught my attention is the takedown system. BLACKWOOD has a huge number of executions, with animations changing depending on the environment and the current situation. And the developers didn't just create them as flashy animations, they used real stunt performers to capture the movements. The intention is for the violence to feel grounded and physical, rather than exaggerated. And you can actually customise that.

As you unlock more takedowns, you can assign them to slots so your executions play out as a sequence that you've chosen. And that's a really strange little feature, but it tells you something about the game's priorities. Blackwood wants combat to feel almost like choreography, not just press button, kill enemy. It wants you to recognise your own style. And this is probably the most important thing about the entire game. The violence means more because it has somewhere to go afterwards.

Imagine finishing a mission, and you've just fought through a building, you've shot people, you've done these ridiculous takedowns, and then you go back to your DVD store. The music changes, the pace slows down, and you stand behind the counter. And someone asks about a film. And for a moment, Anton has to pretend that none of what happened last night even exists. That contrast is the entire fantasy. It's not just, I'm John Wick, it's I'm John Wick.

But tomorrow morning I have to open up the shop And that's far more interesting and relatable Because suddenly the quiet moments aren't filler They're actually the other half of the story And here's the thing that I keep coming back to It's not the guns It's not the takedowns It's actually the routine Wake up Get dressed Open the shop and sell some DVDs Talk to people And then leave Kill someone Come home Upgrade your weapons Pay your bills Go to sleep And repeat

And to some, that sounds incredibly mundane. But that's exactly why I think it could work. Because games normally skip the boring parts of a character's life. They skip the breakfast, the commute, the shop, the ordinary conversations that you have. And they take us straight to the exciting stuff. Blackwood is trying to do the opposite. It's saying that the boring stuff is actually part of the point of the game. Because the boring life is the life Anton is trying to protect.

Every normal day gives meaning to the nights when everything goes wrong. Every dollar earned legitimately represents something that Anton is trying to preserve. And every dirty dollar pushes him further away from it. And suddenly, running the DVD store becomes character development. And the reason I'm watching Blackwood is I don't think it needs to reinvent third-person shooters to work. It doesn't need to have the best gunplay ever made, and it doesn't need to become the next Grand Theft Auto.

It definitely doesn't need to be the next John Wick. What it needs to do is commit to its central idea. That Anton is living two lives. Because if the store genuinely matters, and the relationships, and the money, and the consequences, they all genuinely matter, then the missions become more than isolated action sequences. They're disrupting something. Every time he has to leave that shop, he's putting the other half of his life at risk. And that's the story I want to see.

And there are a lot of games coming out that promise to let us be someone else. A superhero, a soldier, a criminal, an assassin. Blackwood is trying to do something a little bit different. He's asking us to become someone who is trying not to be himself. And that's a mind twister. By day, Anton has a store, he has customers, etc. He has a tiny piece of normality that he can call his own. And by night, he becomes the person that normal life is protecting him from.

And eventually those two worlds do have to collide at some point. And that's what makes it interesting to me. Because all the while you still have to pretend that you're just Anton. Because maybe the most interesting thing about being an assassin isn't killing someone. It's going home afterwards and trying to live like you didn't.
